lens: The most publishable signal here is a metabolic paradox specific to obesity: lean mice show the expected glucagon rise during fasting while obese mice show a glucagon *decrease* (Facts 21-22, J Endocrinology 2019), and IGF-I shifts from −66 µg/l in lean to +27 µg/l in obese during fasting (Fact 8, Am J Physiol-Endocrinol Metab 2018). This means the very population targeted by fasting interventions—obese humans—mountes an inverted hormonal response, yet virtually no Ramadan or intermittent-fasting trials stratify results by BMI subgroup. A second tier of publishability lies in the 72-hour skeletal muscle insulin resistance paradox (Fact 4, Am J Physiol-Endocrinol Metab 2011) colliding with short-term Ramadan glucose improvements (Fact 2) but negligible HbA1c movement (Fact 25), suggesting a biphasic insulin-sensitivity curve whose inflection point remains unmapped.
known_to_ignore: Fasting reduces body weight and BMI in Ramadan studies
Fasting decreases fasting blood sugar in Ramadan studies
Fasting reduces LDL, triglycerides, total cholesterol during Ramadan
Fasting decreases HOMA index and insulin levels acutely
Total body weight and body fat percentage decrease with fasting
tensions: Fact 4 (72-h fast → profound skeletal muscle insulin resistance, Am J Physiol-Endocrinol Metab 2011) vs Facts 2/15-16 (Ramadan fasting → significant FBS and insulin decreases, J Clin Basic Res 2017): prolonged continuous fasting worsens muscle insulin sensitivity while intermittent daily fasting improves systemic glucose — dose–duration axis is uncharacterized

Fact 22 (lean mice: glucagon rises at 24 h) vs Fact 21 (obese DIO mice: glucagon falls between 8–24 h, J Endocrinology 2019): the counter-regulatory glucagon response to fasting is inverted in obesity, contradicting the assumption that fasting physiology is uniform across body composition

Fact 8 (ΔIGF-I: lean −66 µg/l vs obese +27 µg/l during fasting, P < 0.01, Am J Physiol-Endocrinol Metab 2018): IGF-1 suppression — the proposed longevity mechanism of fasting — does not occur in obese subjects, undermining the mechanistic rationale for fasting in obesity

Fact 2 (FBS significantly decreased during Ramadan, P < 0.0001) vs Fact 3 (serum glucose higher during fasting period vs before Ramadan, P < 0.05, Afr J Biotech 2010): same fasting paradigm produces opposite glucose outcomes, likely reflecting diabetic vs non-diabetic subpopulation or week-of-Ramadan timing effects that are never disentangled

Fact 25 (HbA1c only slightly decreased, P < 0.05) vs Fact 2 (large acute FBS reduction): the disconnect between acute fasting glucose improvements and marginal long-term glycemic control (HbA1c) questions whether Ramadan/IF produces durable metabolic benefit or merely transient ketotic dips
gaps: No fact-set data on glucagon dynamics stratified by BMI category in human intermittent-fasting trials — the J Endocrinology 2019 mouse finding has not been replicated in humans during 16:8 or 5:2 protocols

No dose–response mapping between fasting duration (4 h vs 24 h vs 72 h) and skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity in the same cohort; Fact 4's 72-h resistance finding exists in isolation from shorter-protocol data

Bscl2 (seipin) knockout mice show impaired acute insulin signaling after only 4 h of fasting (Fact 18, Endocrinology 2014) — lipodystrophy gene × fasting interaction is unexplored in human partial-lipodystrophy cohorts despite growing GLP-1 agonist overlap

15-F2t-isoprostane (15-FIP) urinary levels rise during fasting (Fact 11, J Nutr Metab 2012), yet no Ramadan or IF trial simultaneously measures oxidative-stress biomarkers alongside glucose/lipid endpoints in the same subjects

Spatial memory correlates inversely with fasting glucose (r_s = 0.56, Fact 12, Aging 2016) but this is from an aging cohort with no fasting intervention — the cognitive domain is absent from the metabolic fasting literature
No data on how the 6-day Phase II steady-state hormonal milieu (Fact 23, Am J Physiol-Regul Integr Comp Physiol 2012) maps onto shorter intermittent-fasting protocols that claim similar benefits

theses.title: Obesity abolishes fasting-induced IGF-1 suppression and inverts the glucagon counter-regulatory response: a mechanistic threat to fasting-for-longevity claims
theses.rationale: Facts 8, 21, and 22 together show that two canonical fasting-mediated protective pathways — IGF-1 reduction and glucagon mobilization — are reversed or absent in obese organisms, yet obesity is the primary indication for fasting interventions. Synthesizing these mechanistic inversions into a coherent review fills a gap no existing narrative review addresses, though the evidence base is thin (two mouse studies, one human IGF-1 sub-analysis).

theses.title: Biphasic insulin-sensitivity response to fasting duration: mapping the inflection point between acute improvement and 72-hour skeletal muscle resistance
theses.rationale: Fact 4 (72-h skeletal muscle insulin resistance) and Facts 2, 15-16 (acute Ramadan glucose improvement) bracket a likely U-shaped curve. A pilot meta-analysis pooling HOMA-IR or glucose clamp data across fasting durations (4 h to 7+ days) from IF trials could identify the duration threshold at which benefits reverse, answering a question the field has not formally posed.

theses.title: Acute fasting glucose improvements do not translate to durable HbA1c reduction in Ramadan intermittent fasting: disconnect meta-regression
theses.rationale: Facts 2 and 25 represent a clinically important divergence — large acute FBS drops coexist with marginal HbA1c changes. A meta-regression of Ramadan IF studies reporting both endpoints, stratified by diabetic status and diabetes medication use, would test whether the acute benefit is pharmacokinetic artifact (timing of metformin/sulfonylurea relative to fasting hours) rather than true metabolic reprogramming.

reviewer_objections: The glucagon and IGF-1 obesity-reversal findings come from mouse models (DIO and lean mice) with no human replication — extrapolation to obese patients undergoing 16:8 or 5:2 fasting protocols is speculative without at least one human clamp study

The 72-h insulin resistance finding (Fact 4) used euglycemic-hyperinsulinemic clamp in a small lab study; generalizing to real-world intermittent fasting (typically ≤ 36 h) conflates a supraphysiological duration with common practice

Ramadan fasting involves not just caloric timing but also dehydration, sleep disruption, and altered meal composition — attributing glucose changes to fasting per se without controlling for confounders is a known methodological weakness across nearly every cited study

The HbA1c disconnect thesis (Fact 25 vs Fact 2) is weakened by the fact that Ramadan is only 29–30 days — insufficient time for HbA1c (120-day RBC lifespan marker) to fully reflect any genuine glycemic improvement
Most source studies have unknown or unreported population descriptors ('pop=?'), making subgroup stratification claims difficult to defend quantitatively
next_extractions: All Ramadan fasting studies that report both FBS and HbA1c, with sample size and diabetic vs non-diabetic stratification, to power the acute-vs-chronic disconnect meta-regression
Human clamp studies or CGM (continuous glucose monitoring) trials of fasting protocols ≥ 48 h to replicate the 72-h insulin resistance finding with modern methodology
Any human data on glucagon or IGF-1 changes during fasting stratified by BMI category (lean < 25 vs overweight 25–30 vs obese > 30), including from FMD (fasting-mimicking diet) trials
Cognitive performance endpoints (spatial memory, executive function) measured alongside glucose/insulin in aging-population fasting trials, to test the Fact 12 correlation prospectively
Oxidative stress biomarkers (8-isoprostane, MDA, SOD) measured concurrently with metabolic panels in any intermittent-fasting RCT, to contextualize the Fact 11 15-FIP finding
